transcript:
Meeting header: date 2026-04-14 11:30 PT, duration ~52m. Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Harborline Head of Data), Tom Larkin (Lead ML Eng), Sara O'Neill (Security).
Summary (auto): high-level discovery: model selection for customer-facing chat + document search, internationalization needs (EN/ES/FR), context window around 8k->32k, tool-calling for payments/checks, hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, SOC2/SSO/KMS concerns, plan to run 1-week benchmark pilot.
----- Transcript -----
00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we only have about 50 minutes so i'll kick us off. quick intros?
00:12 Priya Singh: hi priya here, head of data at harborline, we run a bunch of consumer banking flows and want to add LLM features for chat and document understanding.
00:20 Tom Larkin: tom, lead ml engineer, i'll own the evaluation and integration.
00:24 Sara O'Neill: sara, security architect, i'll be asking the usual compliance questions.
00:28 Diego Ramirez: diego from redwood, infra and runtime, happy to deep dive on latency and deployment options.
00:32 Maya Chen: great, goal for today is model selection and deployment fit — when should we be hosted, dedicated, or private — and get a sense on context length, multilingual and tool calling needs.
01:05 Priya Singh: high level we want a chat assistant on the banking app, doc ingestion for statements, and a backend workflow that can call payment APIs. latency target 400 ms for short chats, okay if some flows are higher. cost target is important though — we have to keep unit cost manageable at scale.
01:40 Tom Larkin: also lots of international users, EN/ES/FR primarily, occasional German and Portuguese. Context length for document search could be up to 20k tokens if we include long statements.
02:02 Sara O'Neill: compliance-wise we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS for key management. data residency: EU for european customers. we have a timeline — pilot in 6 weeks, production Q4.
02:25 Maya Chen: good constraints — thank you. diego, maybe start with model tradeoffs: open model families that meet multilingual & tool-calling needs.
02:36 Diego Ramirez: sure. broadly there are two axes: capability vs cost. open models like the recent 70b and 100b families give strong multilingual generation, better instruction following, and often support tool-calling patterns if you implement structured output. smaller quantized variants (7b/13b) are much cheaper but you hit quality drop, especially on long context. also note the runtime picks quantized kernels for V100/A100/GB100 variants, but accuracy tradeoffs.
03:15 Tom Larkin: when you say tool-calling, do you mean function calling like structured JSON or external tool triggers? we need both — e.g., 'initiate payment' intent that calls our payment service, and also richer structured parsers for statement extraction.
03:30 Diego Ramirez: yes both. hosted supports function-calling via streaming and schema validation, and you can integrate a router to check intent confidence before executing. dedicated gives more control for low latency and private deployments give network isolation — but tool-calling with private requires an outbound egress pattern or connector into your VPC.
04:05 Priya Singh: ok, help us map to hosted/dedicated/private: which is typical for banks?
04:12 Diego Ramirez: enterprise banks usually start with Dedicated for predictable latency and isolation — reserved GPU pools with burst capacity. Private is chosen when policy requires customer-managed control plane and strict VPC-only access. Hosted is fastest to iterate, great for POC, but some banks prefer dedicated due to data handling and SLAs.
05:01 Sara O'Neill: on Private, what's the KMS story? we run keys in our cloud KMS and want HSM-backed...
05:10 Diego Ramirez: we support CMK integrations with major KMS providers and can integrate HSM for key wrapping. audit logs are shipped to your logging endpoint; you can also opt to keep logs on-prem in Private. small caveat: hosted defaults to ephemeral keys managed by redwood unless you bring-your-own-key.
05:45 Tom Larkin: about context windows — you mentioned larger models handle up to 32k tokens, how does tokenization and KV cache behave with long documents?
05:54 Diego Ramirez: runtime maintains kv cache for attention state; for long documents we recommend chunking + embedding-based retrieval for doc search to avoid feeding entire doc in single prompt. For QA over statements, you can use a 32k model if needed but cost and latency increase; we typically recommend 8k-16k for interactive chat and an RAG approach for >16k.
06:30 Priya Singh: we have two user flows: quick chat (short context, high qps) and deep statement analysis (lower qps, high context). sounds like hybrid approach?
06:45 Maya Chen: yes hybrid — smaller quantized 8k model for chat, larger 32k for deep analysis or batch processing. diego, how big is the difference in cost and latency between hosted 8k quantized vs hosted 32k full precision?
07:05 Diego Ramirez: rough ballpark: quantized 8k can be 3-6x cheaper per token and lower latency due to smaller memory and better batching. 32k full precision often needs higher tier GPUs and memory, latency can be 2-3x higher per request. but caching and batching policies can reduce token cost for the 32k path if requests share prefixes.
07:40 Tom Larkin: any recommended models we should benchmark? open model list suggestions please.
07:47 Diego Ramirez: sure — Mistral/Orca-family forks are good for instruction, we also see strong multi-lingual from certain community optimized LMs like Polyglot-3 and some emergent open 70b models. For 32k, look at variants where the community has trained longcontext adapters or use LlamaX-style extended context builds. We'll provide a catalog with perf profiles.
08:20 Priya Singh: are hallucinations better on bigger models? we need fact-checking for payments — false positives could be bad.
08:30 Diego Ramirez: bigger models usually reduce some hallucination but not eliminate; important to add retrieval-augmented generation and structured validation. For payments, add deterministic checks and intent confirmation prompts, and gate API calls behind confidence thresholds and human-in-the-loop for high risk.
09:05 Sara O'Neill: log retention and PII: we cannot retain raw statements in hosted logs. what's the redwood recommended pattern?
09:16 Maya Chen: good question. redwood supports configurable redaction at ingest; for hosted most customers use de-identification and token-level anonymization. Private allows you to keep raw payloads inside your VPC and only surface metrics. We'll share the technical note.
09:40 Tom Larkin: on multilingual quality — do we need separate models per language or one general multilingual?
09:48 Diego Ramirez: one multilingual model is simpler operationally and often performs well, but sometimes single-language fine-tuned models outperform on subtle grammar/locale phrasing. We recommend start with a multilingual candidate, then evaluate per-language eval sets. Dedicated allows you to run different models per route if needed.
10:20 Priya Singh: timeline again — pilot in 6 weeks. what does pilot look like?
10:28 Maya Chen: pilot = 1 week of benchmark runs + a small live canary with real traffic routing to a dedicated pool, evaluate latency, cost, and quality metrics. we normally do a pilot SOW to scope data, success metrics, and rollback criteria.
10:45 Tom Larkin: for benchmarks, what inputs do you need?
10:49 Diego Ramirez: sample prompts in production distribution, anonymized logs, representative documents, and a list of endpoints we plan to tool-call. we also need QPS targets and latency SLOs to size GPUs.
11:08 Priya Singh: can you run the benchmark in our region (eu-west-1) — data residency?
11:14 Diego Ramirez: yes, Dedicated and Private can be provisioned in eu-west-1. Hosted is available in multi-region but for strict residency we recommend Dedicated in-region or Private.
11:35 Sara O'Neill: encryption at rest and in transit?
11:38 Diego Ramirez: TLS for in transit, at-rest encryption via KMS. Private allows you to control keys. We support bring-your-own-key in Dedicated as well.
12:00 Tom Larkin: what about autoscaling — bursts during payday spikes?
12:05 Diego Ramirez: Dedicated supports autoscaling and burst capacity. we can configure warm pools for predicted spikes; Private has similar options depending on infra constraints. we also offer knobbed batching to keep latency stable under bursts.
12:35 Priya Singh: do you have any customer references in banking?
12:40 Maya Chen: we have a couple of financial services customers on Dedicated and Private — will share anonymized case studies and latency/cost numbers.
12:55 Tom Larkin: integration complexity — we use OAuth2 and internal service mesh for tool calls. how does Redwood attach to our APIs?
13:03 Diego Ramirez: you can register callbacks with JWT-signed requests or use a connector inside your VPC for Private. For Dedicated we support mutual TLS or short-lived signed tokens.
13:25 Sara O'Neill: audit logs — want detailed request/response metadata but not full user content. can you redact request bodies?
13:33 Diego Ramirez: yes, configurable logging filters; we can redact or hash PII fields before storage and stream structured metrics to your SIEM.
14:02 Priya Singh: question on model versioning and rollouts — feature flags for model variants?
14:09 Maya Chen: redwood console supports model pinning, canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies if a variant fails. You can route by route or by user cohort.
14:40 Tom Larkin: okay, costs — can you share an example pricing for dedicated reserved pool vs hosted?
14:48 Maya Chen: we'll share a dedicated pricing template in the SOW. hosted is usage-based per token and embedding, dedicated has reserved vGPU costs plus usage. we'll put example numbers in the follow-up.
15:10 Priya Singh: any compliance docs we can digest quickly?
15:15 Maya Chen: yes SOC2, ISO, encryption plus our deployment playbook — we'll attach.
15:28 Tom Larkin: on the technical bench, Diego you mentioned caching and prefix sharing — can you quickly explain how that reduces cost?
15:35 Diego Ramirez: if many requests share system prompts or task instructions we keep those in cache/KV and avoid recomputing attention for those tokens. that reduces generated tokens and compute cycles. it's most effective for chatbots with consistent system prompts.
16:05 Priya Singh: ok that helps. last part — failures and graceful degradation?
16:12 Diego Ramirez: we support automatic fallback to a smaller model or to a cached response. for mission-critical ops like payments, we recommend an approval step before execution and keep synchronous fallback endpoints.
16:35 Maya Chen: let's recap next steps and owners. Priya — share prompts and logs by 2026-04-18. Maya — send pricing and SOW by 2026-04-16. Diego — benchmark config by 2026-04-20. Sara — compliance checklist by 2026-04-18. we schedule a pilot kickoff after data lands.
17:08 Priya Singh: sounds good. quick clarifying q: for the statement parser do you recommend starting with a 32k model or RAG?
17:16 Diego Ramirez: start with RAG + a mid-size long-context model for edge cases. it reduces cost and gives more precise retrieval results.
17:40 Tom Larkin: ok thanks everyone.
17:45 Maya Chen: all right we'll follow up with the SOW and docs. thanks all.
17:52 Meeting end.

Notes: transcript has occasional transcription errors and shorthand (e.g., 'kv cache' transcribed as 'kay vee cache' in spots), some speaker labels conflated in automated feed.
